# Sirach Chapter 31 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic Equivalence)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Sirach 31 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/SIR_031_page_001.jpg

---

**31:1** Worrying about wealth can wear a person to the bone, and the anxiety it brings will keep you awake at night.

**31:2** Restless worry destroys your sleep, and a serious illness will take it away just the same.

**31:3** The rich man wears himself out piling up wealth, and when he finally stops, he stuffs himself with luxuries.

**31:4** The poor man wears himself out just getting by, and when he rests, he is still in need.

**31:5** No one who is obsessed with gold can be called righteous, and chasing after money will only lead you astray.

**31:6** Many people have been ruined by gold — their destruction came to meet them head-on.

**31:7** Gold is a trap for those who are devoted to it, and every fool will be caught by it.

**31:8** How fortunate is the wealthy person who is found to be blameless, who has not gone running after money!

**31:9** Who is such a person? We would congratulate them, for they have done something truly remarkable among their people.

**31:10** Who has faced the test and come through unscathed? That is something to be proud of. Who had the opportunity to do wrong and refused, to cause harm and held back?

**31:11** Such a person's good fortune will last, and people will celebrate their generosity in public.

**31:12** When you sit down to dinner at an important person's table, don't start gulping everything in sight. Don't say, "Look at all this food!"

**31:13** Remember — a greedy eye is a wicked thing. Nothing was made more wicked than the eye; that's why it weeps from every face.

**31:14** Don't reach for everything your eye falls on, and don't crowd your neighbor at the serving dish.

**31:15** Judge how your neighbor feels by how you would feel in their place, and be thoughtful about everything you do.

**31:16** Eat whatever is placed in front of you the way a well-brought-up person would, and don't wolf it down greedily — you don't want people to dislike you.

**31:17** Be the first to stop eating, as a matter of good manners. Don't overindulge, or people will take offense.

**31:18** If you're dining with many others, don't be the one who reaches before everyone else.

**31:19** For someone with self-discipline, a little is quite enough; such a person sleeps soundly.

**31:20** Moderation at the table means healthy sleep; the person gets up early feeling sharp and clear. But the glutton suffers insomnia, nausea, and stomach cramps.

**31:21** If you've been forced to eat too much, excuse yourself, step outside, get it out of your system — you'll feel much better.

**31:22** Listen to me, child — don't dismiss what I'm saying. In the end, you'll see I was right. In everything you do, be disciplined, and illness will pass you by.

**31:23** The generous host earns everyone's praise, and his good reputation is well-deserved.

**31:24** The stingy host earns the whole town's complaint, and his bad reputation is equally well-deserved.

**31:25** Don't try to prove your strength by drinking wine — wine has been the undoing of many.

**31:26** Fire tests steel in the forge; and wine tests character when proud people start to argue.

**31:27** Wine is one of life's great gifts when you drink it sensibly. What kind of life is there without wine? It was made to bring people joy.

**31:28** Drunk at the right time and in the right amount, wine brings cheerfulness to the heart and lightness to the soul.

**31:29** But drunk to excess, wine turns bitter — it stirs up arguments and makes people fall flat on their faces.

**31:30** Too much wine inflames the anger of a fool, to his own detriment — it saps his strength and adds to his injuries.

**31:31** Don't scold your neighbor when you're both at a dinner party, and don't put him down when he's enjoying himself. Don't say anything cutting to him, and don't pester him with demands.
